claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary single-phase FCC alloys result from differences in local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion alters stacking-fault energy.
Local structural differences promote different degrees of chemical short-range order.
Variations in stacking-fault energy and chemical short-range order modulate dislocation mobility and slip behavior.
Changes in dislocation mobility and slip behavior govern alloy strength and ductility.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline can be prepared as a single-phase FCC alloy by thermomechanical processing.
Compositional changes modify effective atomic-volume mismatch.
Changes in effective atomic-volume mismatch produce spatial fluctuations in lattice parameters.
Local stacking-fault-energy variations affect dislocation nucleation, mobility, and slip-system activation.
Quaternary and ternary alloys with greater atomic mismatch than Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni will have higher strength and hardness.
The predicted increase in strength and hardness arises from enhanced lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening.
Quaternary and ternary alloys with greater atomic mismatch may have lower ductility because dislocation motion is constrained.
Strength, hardness, and ductility trends will correlate with measured stacking-fault energies and local lattice distortions.
The proposed mechanism applies only to thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys.
The mechanism may not govern mechanical response in multiphase alloys or where grain-boundary effects and processing-induced defects dominate.
Grain-boundary character, nanoprecipitates, and dislocation substructures may significantly influence the measured mechanical properties.
Greater lattice distortion together with lower stacking-fault energy should produce higher strength and hardness but lower ductility.
